reviews.text:
My parakeet became ill and I took him to my regular vet, but his condition worsened. Since my regular vet was closed, I called this clinic urgently. Despite being fully booked, they managed to squeeze me in.

Immediately after the examination, they informed me, in a considerate manner, that it wasn't the illness diagnosed at my regular vet.

It was gastroenteritis and pneumonia. Because he wouldn't take his medication, he quickly became critically ill and was hospitalized, but he recovered successfully.

The hospitalization fee was only the amount initially quoted. Therefore, I think this is an honest clinic that doesn't perform unnecessary tests.

I am truly grateful for their help. Thank you very much.

I have discarded my previous vet's medical card.

I've been a patient here since this hospital opened.

Sometimes the doctor's tone can be stern, but I believe that's because he's thinking about the parakeets' well-being.

Also, when my parakeet developed moderate pneumonia due to my poor care, they treated it as an outpatient rather than hospitalizing it, and prescribed the appropriate medication, which allowed it to recover completely. I can't thank them enough.

To ensure I can properly care for these birds I've welcomed into my home, I intend to continue using this hospital's services.

True experience, medical clinic has certain requirements, one-time medical service, responsibility, and medical clinic!

The book is a medical treatment that is a favorite of the sick, because of the physical condition of the heart, and the ability to achieve professional treatment.

As a result, I went to the hospital, completed the examination, opened a private room, and asked my family to visit the home?

Check it out? Observation of illness? Return to death?

How do you understand the treatment, do you want to say it indirectly? Is it time to visit a competent hospital?

The owner is not a doctor, I am not happy because of the cause, and the talent association is selected to cooperate with your business!

How do you know if you have the ability to do the job, notify the sincerity of the offer, and make unnecessary indulgences?

I'm here at the hospital, but only one of them is suffering from many illnesses, but I'm here, and I'm a family member!

Most people's atmosphere is negative, medical law is not protected, and the situation is clear.

Life isn't something you gamble on, and it certainly can't be easily handled with a simple "take it home and observe"!

I truly realized how crucial it is to choose a trustworthy and responsible animal hospital.

My beloved pet was unwell, and I took it to the hospital out of concern. I desperately wanted it to get better, to receive appropriate treatment.

But instead, the hospital performed tests, prescribed medication, and sent me home with the instruction to "observe it at home."

What exactly am I supposed to observe?

Am I supposed to watch its condition worsen?

Or am I supposed to wait for it to die?

If they lacked confidence in treating it, they should have been honest.

If they found it difficult to handle, shouldn't they have recommended transferring me to a hospital with specialized treatment?

We pet owners are not veterinarians.

It is precisely because we lack specialized knowledge that we trust veterinarians and entrust the lives of our precious family members to them. If you can't help, at least tell us honestly. Don't waste a precious life.

To the hospital, it may be just one of many animals they see every day.

But to us, it's an irreplaceable and precious member of our family.

We understand that doctors can't always cure everything.

However, despite bringing our pet to the hospital in a worrying state, we were sent home after only tests and a prescription, told to "wait and see." We feel strong doubt and anger.

A life is not something to be left to chance.

We don't think this is a problem that can be easily dismissed with just the words, "wait and see at home."

I visited the clinic for a check-up of my 10-year-old Quaker parrot. Some people might be worried after reading online reviews, but my experience there was completely different.

The head veterinarian is very reliable and considerate, prioritizing the bird's well-being and cost above all else, and doesn't push unnecessary tests.

I would definitely like to entrust the care of any new pets I welcome into my family in the future.

I took my cockatiel to the vet because I was worried about its sneezing. The doctor was a woman.

She weighed it, but didn't tell me the number, so when I asked for clarification, she weighed it again.

She was curt and mechanical, and when I asked her to trim its nails short, she said it would hurt if they bled.

I'm glad I switched to the hospital in Suminoe.
This is the hospital I always go to.

We welcomed a one-month-old budgie, a Harlequin Lutino, into our home.

We were worried because she seemed lethargic after we brought her home, but after a checkup, we discovered she had megabacteria and malnutrition, and we started taking her to the vet.

She regained her energy from the very first visit and is now very healthy!

Thank you so much for the thorough examination and treatment.

We are truly grateful that you helped our precious Himawari get well.

Thank you so much, Director!

I took my Java sparrow to the vet. We went for about six months. The vet was a woman, but she spoke in a very detached manner. She changed the medication without any explanation. Even though it was sick, it ate and looked healthy, but after that it couldn't fly, couldn't walk, and eventually died. I wanted a more empathetic approach to the care of the owner. I will never go there again.

I went there as an emergency case, but they didn't point out any fault on my part as the owner and treated my bird immediately.

They were very gentle in their handling of the bird; even when it was squawking and struggling, they spoke to it kindly and held it gently!

My usual vet told me to wait and see, but I wasn't reassured, so I called this clinic. After listening to my explanation, they were able to see my bird right away because they were worried about it, which made me very happy.

I want to make this my regular vet!

The price is also cheaper compared to other vets!

My four-month-old pet bird suddenly started vomiting severely one day. It was a Saturday evening, and I searched for a bird specialist hospital that was open; this was the only one.

My husband called and explained the symptoms, and they told us to come as soon as possible, allowing us to have an emergency appointment. We managed to arrive about 30 minutes before closing time.

The examination revealed megabacteria (Macrorhabdus ornithogaster), requiring medication and ongoing treatment.

The initial visit, being an emergency, cost approximately 16,800 yen, including examination, tests, and treatment. While it seemed a bit expensive at first, considering my bird's condition was quite serious and they were able to see us despite it being close to closing time, I'm truly grateful this hospital was open.

Subsequent follow-up visits cost approximately 4,500 yen, including examination, injections, and medication for home use. We are still continuing treatment.

The clinic was very clean and had a calm atmosphere, and the other pet owners we met in the waiting room were all very kind. The doctor in charge is very kind.

I'm from Canada, and my Japanese isn't perfect yet. Sometimes I go to the clinic alone when my husband is at work, but they are very kind and helpful, translating explanations into English when necessary. I'm truly grateful for their kindness despite the language barrier.

However, there's one thing I'd like to see improved.

Currently, the only way to make appointments or inquiries is by phone; there are no written communication methods such as LINE, email, inquiry forms, or online booking.

This is one of the few bird-specialized hospitals in Osaka, and I believe many pet owners rely on it when their birds suddenly become ill. Therefore, having at least one contact method other than phone would make it much easier to use.

A phone-only system can be a significant barrier for people with hearing or speech impairments, those who have difficulty processing spoken information, and others who have difficulty with real-time phone communication. Furthermore, phone communication can be particularly difficult for non-native Japanese speakers.

I myself have to ask my husband to call the hospital every time I need to contact them, and sometimes he can't get through immediately if he's at work.

I understand that phone calls are necessary in emergencies, but it would be incredibly helpful if there were at least one way to contact them by text, such as email, LINE, or an online form, for non-emergency appointments and inquiries.

I would really appreciate it if you would consider improving this point, but I am very grateful to the hospital and the doctors. They examined and treated my beloved bird during a very anxious time, and they were also very kind to me despite the language barrier.

In the future, I would be happy if you could introduce contact methods other than phone calls so that more pet owners can use your services with peace of mind.

Thank you so much for taking care of my bird up until now.

He's a bird specialist, but his personality and skills are lacking.
I'm grateful that he saved my beloved bird when it was on the verge of death.
However, the head veterinarian conducted examinations with a gangster-like, oppressive attitude, blaming me for every single mistake I made as the owner.
I felt like my precious pet was being held hostage, and I had no choice but to endure it.
From the examination room, where I could hear everything they were saying, he treated the elderly couple with courtesy, but to me, who was there alone, he was relentlessly oppressive, openly frowning at any questions I didn't expect and responding in a harsh tone.
It was not the kind of attitude you'd expect from a pet owner.

To top it all off, 20 days after he told me he was finished with the medication and examination, I lost my pet.
When I brought him in, an hour's journey, because he didn't seem well, he didn't even take an X-ray.
He just said, "This bird is weak in [specific area]," and did nothing more than a physical examination.
My sweet little bird passed away two days later. I took my bird there on the day it died because it was weak.
However, there was absolutely no apology for the negligence two days prior.
While hoping that more bird specialist hospitals with kind and skilled staff will open in Osaka,
I will not keep any more birds because I don't want to experience such sadness again.
Even if I were to get a bird, I would not bring it here.
If you want your precious pet to live a long life, I do not recommend this hospital.

[Addendum]
Although the head veterinarian did not give any explanation, I believe my bird had megabacteriosis.
I find it inexplicable that they stopped treatment despite this.
I suspect that certain cases or families who don't get along with the head veterinarian are being used as guinea pigs.
This doctor changes his attitude depending on the family of the patient.
If you feel even the slightest bit uneasy, I recommend changing hospitals.

It was Kana-chan's first visit to the vet for a nail trim and checkup. She was nervous, but everything was fine, which was a relief! 👌✨
The doctor was so kind, I'm really grateful! 🙇✨ …

I am especially grateful to the vet for taking my budgie, who had severe pneumonia, to the emergency room and helping him recover (I later learned that he wouldn't have survived if we had been a few hours later). He was my most affectionate bird. The vet was a woman who helped both me and my bird many times and gave me advice on numerous matters. The illness lasted for about three months due to its severity, but this was as the vet had predicted (the first three visits were every two to three days, then gradually became once a week, once every two weeks, and once every three weeks). There were ups and downs in his condition and changes in medication along the way, but each time I received appropriate treatment and guidance, and thanks to that, he gradually recovered. After four months, he was able to talk and play again, and finally, after five months, he was completely back to his healthy, pre-illness state. I also take him to the vet for health checkups, and I have brought a total of 10 budgies there so far. My reason for visiting this clinic was that a bird I had previously had developed megabacteria, and the treatment at the previous hospital was ineffective, so I sought a second opinion.

The doctor doesn't just give templated answers like those found in books; he provides treatment and information based on his own experience. He also shared various tips on bird care and discussed the latest medical advances. He sometimes provides additional information on topics that he finds particularly interesting during subsequent visits. Even when I visited for treatment of another bird, he checked in on its condition and even called me through a staff member.

The three staff members are incredibly kind and attentive. They are always smiling, speak gently, and listen carefully to what you have to say, which is a great support for pet owners who are anxious about visiting the clinic.

I've seen several reviews mentioning the doctor's cold tone or blaming the owner for their shortcomings, so I wanted to share my own experience.

I've also found them to be incredibly kind. On one occasion, the food and water had spilled during transport, making a mess inside the cage. They kindly cleaned the cage and refilled it (this may also be due to the staff's quick thinking). When my bird wasn't feeling well, they kept it warm in the treatment room while I waited for my appointment. After the examination, they also kept it in the treatment room for a short time to check on it, as moving it immediately could cause vomiting. They were also considerate of my multiple birds, asking, "Isn't it difficult to bring multiple birds in for checkups every day? Shall we arrange an appointment for a day when we can see all of them at once?"

I was never treated aggressively or blamed; on the contrary, they expressed concern about my living environment, such as the temperature and any odor (because several of my birds had developed pneumonia and gastrointestinal problems due to the cold). They gently and kindly told me, with a worried expression, "Please review your living environment once again to make sure it's okay."

While I can honestly say that occasionally his tone can seem cold, he never changes his attitude depending on the patient, and it's clear that he genuinely cares deeply for the birds and dedicates himself to their well-being. I see him as a very cool and dedicated bird caretaker.

I myself have been told quite bluntly things like, "I've explained this many times before. Since you have multiple birds, I understand you might be confused, so please take notes," or "Could you please prepare your questions in advance so that it doesn't interfere with the next patient?" These comments stung, but when I sincerely apologized, he blushed and said, "I'm the one who should apologize. I didn't mean to blame you, so I hope you understand," showing that he's a pure-hearted person with no ill intentions whatsoever. If he truly disliked patients, he would only provide the necessary treatment and wouldn't offer any further information. I was once told, "You always ask me a lot of questions, but I don't have time today because I have an emergency patient and surgery scheduled later." While this statement can be hurtful if taken literally, I myself was there for an emergency that day, and I was greatly relieved by the quick and appropriate treatment I received (the day I rushed there with my severely ill budgie, as mentioned at the beginning). So, I'm actually grateful.

As a medical institution, it's natural for them to strive to ensure smooth consultations in case of emergencies, so I understand that those words probably came out naturally in that situation. If there are emergency patients or surgeries before or after, the doctor's tension must increase, and they might unintentionally raise their voice. There's no doubt that they are a very conscientious and dedicated person.

I took my 10-year-old Java sparrow to the vet for the first time because I was worried about its eyes. I could really feel the doctor's love for birds. Not only was the examination thorough, but they didn't recommend any unnecessary treatments. They also advised on age-appropriate nutritional balance and recommended commercially available vitamins, which I found incredibly thoughtful.

I felt this was a trustworthy doctor. Thank you.

I took my bird in for a health checkup.

The doctor was very experienced in handling birds, and I felt at ease during the examination. I'm grateful for all the advice I received.

I drove there, and there was a coin parking lot right next to the hospital, which I used.
He has saved my pet's life twice. He is a very knowledgeable doctor about birds. He is a very direct doctor, so some people might find him harsh, but his skills are undeniable.

I highly recommend this clinic to anyone in Osaka struggling to find a place to treat their bird.

Because it specializes in birds, all the customers are bird owners who cherish their birds, which made me feel very safe and secure in the environment.

The veterinarian is very knowledgeable and explained everything clearly, including past cases, which greatly reduced my anxiety.

My bird is gradually recovering, and I'm so glad I chose this clinic.
This is a very trustworthy hospital.

This hospital has saved my pet so many times, and I'm so glad I chose to bring them here! Initially, I had the impression that it would be expensive based on online reviews, but in my case, even the first visit never cost tens of thousands of yen. Those with pet insurance can claim reimbursement from their insurance company. Approximate treatment costs are listed under [Amount].


[Reason for Visiting]
My budgie was diagnosed with megabacteria infection at a previous hospital and I had been taking him there for a long time. However, he started vomiting and his condition worsened, so I sought a second opinion at this hospital. The previous hospital said the bacteria had disappeared, but tests at this hospital showed they hadn't disappeared at all, revealing that the previous hospital's treatment was ineffective. Since then, I've switched to this hospital and bring in multiple birds for checkups and other treatments.


[Impression]
I was truly impressed; this is a specialized bird hospital! They have multiple medications for even a single illness, and they compound the appropriate medication according to the symptoms, body type, and constitution. If inflammation, gastritis, or nutritional supplements are needed, they also compound those (in a mixed powder form, sometimes including herbal medicine). If there is no improvement, they will adjust the dosage, add or remove medications, etc., during the follow-up consultation at the next visit. In a typical animal hospital, they would probably only prescribe one or two medications plus an injection, and if there is still no improvement, they would be at a loss. Whether treatment is necessary or not, they clearly state this at the first visit, which was very helpful. For animals that require treatment, they provide an estimate of the duration and cost of visits beforehand, explain the necessary treatments, and ultimately guide the decision to the owner. In my case, I told them I did not want hospitalization or surgery, and they respected my wishes without showing any displeasure. I never felt that they were trying to force me to visit or receive treatment or to take my money. My attending veterinarian was the vice-director (female). She is very young and humble, saying, "I will do everything I can to help this animal get better, but my treatment plan and choices are not necessarily always correct." However, she has passed a difficult exam to become a certified member of the Avian Clinical Research Association, and is very knowledgeable and experienced. For animals with no particular problems, the consultation ends with, "I recommend regular checkups as much as possible." Regarding the severely ill child, I called many times during treatment out of anxiety, but each time they listened to my concerns and provided emotional support for us pet owners. When I had many questions, they called me back and answered them carefully. There was also a time when the symptoms could no longer be controlled with medication alone, and they prescribed emergency medication in an emergency. Because the symptoms were severe when we switched to this clinic, the child with severe megabacteria ultimately passed away, but instead of dying within a day or two as expected, they survived for more than a month. Even though the doctor was in the middle of an examination when I called, the receptionist immediately connected me to the doctor, who offered condolences and apologized, saying, "I'm sorry we couldn't do more." Although the child was quite weak and nearing death, the fact that they passed away on the night of the first visit seemed to have shocked the doctor as well, and he offered condolences and apologized again at the next visit. "While it's important to check up on the other birds' health, please take it easy for a while," she said, showing concern for me and my family, but I was struck by how distraught she looked—so much so that I was worried about her. Just like with human hospitals, I think there's a matter of compatibility between the doctor and the patient. Everyone's experience is different, but I've decided to continue bringing my bird to this clinic.


[Fees]
There's a price list in the waiting room and examination room, so you can check your budget beforehand. Pet insurance is accepted. While they'll tell you the approximate costs of various treatments if you call to make an appointment, you should understand that they can't determine what tests are necessary until they actually examine your bird. The following prices are all for small birds as of April 2026 (excluding tax). The initial consultation fee is ¥2,000 per bird, and the follow-up consultation fee (second visit onwards) is ¥1,000. For a simple health check, a crop examination costs ¥500, a stool examination costs ¥500, X-ray examinations have no limit on the number of images and cost ¥6,000 for the first time, and ¥3,000 for subsequent X-rays from the second visit onwards, if prescription medication is required, powdered medication to be mixed with drinking water costs ¥200-¥300 per day, varying depending on the type and dosage (it is generally prescribed assuming 50cc of drinking water, so please let us know if you prefer 25cc. Liquid medication administered directly costs ¥1,000-¥2,000 per bottle (varies depending on the number of days, type of medication, number of times per day, and dosage)), and hospital-made vitamin solution costs ¥900 (one drop per day in 25cc of drinking water, so it lasts quite a while for small numbers of birds. Nekton can be used as a substitute, but hospital-made may be necessary depending on the prescription medication). Injections during visits cost ¥1,000 per dose (antibiotics). (Contains gastrointestinal medication, vitamins, etc.) In the case of megabacteria, liquid antifungal medication may be prescribed, costing around ¥2,000 to ¥3,000 (for severe cases, the dosage is higher, so about 1-2 weeks' worth; for mild cases, more than a month's worth). Even for the same species of bird and the same disease, the type of prescribed medication may differ depending on the severity of symptoms and the bird's constitution, and the price may also fluctuate depending on the increase or decrease in dosage, so this is for reference only. There are also advantageous bird check-up plans that include multiple tests such as blood tests and X-rays, so it is a good idea to take advantage of the discount system. Bird check-up fees differ between weekdays and weekends/holidays, with weekdays being more affordable.

[About the staff]
2 veterinarians, 2 nurses, 1 animal care staff (as of April 2026). You can request a specific veterinarian, but there is a fee. According to the reception, they don't assign veterinarians based on bird species or symptoms; the assigned veterinarian is determined by the availability of staff on your first visit. After that, the same veterinarian will be assigned each time. After the end of each day's consultations, both the head veterinarian and the deputy head veterinarian check all the charts and exchange information, so they are aware of information about birds they are not directly assigned to.

[Important points before visiting]
Advance reservations are mandatory and must be made by phone (no online reservations). Even in emergencies, walk-ins without a reservation are not accepted. Even existing patients must make a reservation if they haven't already scheduled their next appointment. If you wish to have multiple birds seen on the same day, you must inform them in advance (depending on availability, it may be necessary to visit on separate days). (In some cases) Due to measures against infectious diseases such as avian influenza, rescued birds must have been kept in captivity for more than one year. Wild birds are not accepted. Health checkups are also available. To schedule the consultation time based on the symptoms and desired tests, please provide as much detail as possible regarding the bird's species, sex, age, symptoms, reason for visit, etc. (For health checkups, please specify whether you would like simple tests such as crop fluid or fecal tests, or more detailed tests such as bird checkups). First-time patients and existing patients bringing a new bird will need to fill out a questionnaire (the questionnaire can be downloaded from our official website. Bringing a printed and completed form in advance will make the process smoother). Please arrive 15 minutes before your scheduled appointment time to allow time for data entry by the reception staff. Yes.

[Precautions within the hospital]
Never open the birdcage in the waiting room. To prevent injury and infection, absolutely do not let your bird come into contact with other patients' birds. Since some birds may panic, cover the birdcage or carrier with a towel or similar material so that they cannot see each other. Ensure proper insulation. The doctor will also open and close the birdcage in the examination room.

[Challenges at the hospital]
On days when appointments are fully booked, you may be simply told to "consider visiting another medical institution," which I think is a challenge. Because there are only two veterinarians and many patients, it is often difficult to get through on the phone to make an appointment, and it is common for desired dates to be unavailable or for appointments to be booked several days in advance. There are no concerning symptoms, and for those considering a health check-up, we recommend making an appointment well in advance. However, they seem to have a minimum system in place to accept emergency birds, although this is limited to their operating hours. Currently, they have more days off than average (compared to a certain bird specialist hospital in northern Osaka), with two days off per week plus several additional unscheduled days per month. This is apparently due to the need to allocate time for surgeries and the management of hospitalized birds. They are currently recruiting veterinarians, so we hope this will be resolved in the future. As a relatively new hospital (opened in January 2024), they are likely still learning and striving to improve, so we expect things to get better in the future.

[Hospital Overview]
A specialist hospital for pet birds, opened in January 2024. Reservations are required by phone in advance. It's close to Teradacho Station on the JR Osaka Loop Line, but it's located a little way down a side street. You might get a little lost the first time you go, so allow plenty of time. Many people seem to arrive by car or taxi. Bicycle parking is available. No car parking is available. It's a ground-floor tenant in the newly built 8-story apartment building, "Tennoji Route 25".


[Advice from a Veterinarian]
Infections are increasing among budgies acquired from pet shops and breeders. Megabacteriosis is particularly common, with a high success rate of around 70-80%, so it's best to assume infection. It can be detected with a simple health check (fecal examination), so it's best to get it checked as early as possible. It's best to have your bird examined at least once (ideally before it turns one year old; the earlier the better). There's no need to give up just because it's infected; with early and appropriate treatment, there's a high chance of complete recovery (the younger the bird, the higher the recovery rate, especially if it's asymptomatic. Even if the bacteria disappear, birds with symptoms like vomiting may be left with gastritis as a sequela). If you have the financial means, a bird checkup including various infectious disease tests is recommended as soon as you bring your bird home. Recently, there has been an increasing trend of birds infected with BFD (a disease affecting budgie chicks). It's a scary disease that can be fatal before the bird turns one year old, but it can be prevented if detected before symptoms appear, so it's recommended to have various infectious disease tests (bird checkup) done as soon as possible after bringing your bird home.

The head veterinarian's attitude was terrible. I was worried about my beloved bird and had many questions, but he completely dismissed everything I said and treated me with contempt. My bird's condition worsened while I was going to this hospital, so I went to another hospital and it recovered smoothly. I'm so glad I switched hospitals.

I'm so glad we were able to have our bird examined by this doctor.
I have a conure, but after my work situation changed and I started spending more time alone, it began plucking its feathers. Another hospital prescribed antidepressants, but after a month there was no sign of improvement, so after much deliberation, I found this hospital for a second opinion. The doctor listened carefully to what we had to say, observed our bird thoroughly, and then examined it gently, speaking to it kindly. They also suggested many ways to improve the situation.
They corrected some of the mistakes I had learned from YouTube and other sources, while being supportive of us, and I learned a lot from my own mistakes. This doctor is truly wonderful and genuinely cares about the happiness of birds. It's a bit far, but I would like to continue to ask this doctor for help in the future.
This hospital provides very kind and attentive care.
Our birds are cared for here. The vet is very knowledgeable about birds (which is to be expected). Our birds are healthy, and the fees are reasonable, which is a great help.

I found you on Twitter and have been seeing you since December, traveling four hours each way. My next appointment was on February 1st, but on Saturday, January 24th, I lost my budgie. He was 9 years old. Until then, you had me check on him carefully once a month.
I was taking medication and his appetite had started to improve, so I'm still in shock and haven't been able to process it, but I'm very grateful. The more I think about it, the more I regret it, but I'm grateful that you were there to treat him.
It was a short time, but thank you very much.

I visited the clinic for the first time yesterday.

Unfortunately, my bird was diagnosed with terminal cancer.

However, the doctor explained everything thoroughly, allowing us to make choices that would make my bird as comfortable as possible. I felt that the doctor truly loves birds, as my bird seemed completely at ease and comfortable around him. I regret not noticing his illness sooner and visiting this hospital earlier.

My wife came to see us because our bird was not feeling well. Apparently, they pointed out to her in a very strong tone that it was partly her fault that the bird was not well. When she tried to explain that she had been unable to do the service due to hospitalization, she was interrupted by an even stronger and more overbearing tone. She said she took the advice seriously, but cried, saying that there was a better way to respond or express things. There have been several similar comments, but it seems that all critical reviews are deleted. Please be aware of this.

I'm grateful that they found a disease that other hospitals hadn't found.

However, when I answered when they asked if there was anything different, they found fault with me as the owner and started to put a lot of pressure on me, which was scary.

They half-laughed and said, "I explained this to you before, didn't I?", which I was confused because I had already done that. But even so, they didn't seem to remember what I had said before.

But they didn't help me think of a solution, they just said, "Other people are able to do it," and in the end we couldn't find a solution.

I ended up leaving feeling frustrated. I wish I hadn't asked the question. I don't want to go there again if possible. I'll look for another hospital.

I was worried about the leg of my 8-month-old Call Duck and took him to the vet for the first time. I was having trouble finding a hospital that would see him, but this bird specialist hospital was fantastic. They examined him thoroughly, and my worries were relieved.

I had only been able to get information about his diet from the internet, but they also gave me nutritional guidance, which was very helpful. They answered all my questions clearly and confidently; I feel very reassured by their doctor.

The doctor was a man, and I think he might have been the head doctor (I forgot to ask). I'll definitely use their services again if needed.

I visited the clinic for the first time last summer and was given the option of surgery or medication. After much deliberation, I decided on surgery.
During my hospital stay, I was kept updated on my condition by phone and was treated very kindly.
As other reviewers have said, the medical fees are higher than other places but I think this is reasonable given the location.
I have continued to visit the clinic every month since being discharged, and the director has a great love for birds. He speaks to them gently and I feel at ease during his examinations.
There are no bird-specializing hospitals nearby, so it takes five hours round trip, which is difficult, but I would like to continue receiving treatment from him.

Although my conure isn't sick, I take him to Bird Dog every six months for a health checkup.

He's treated by a female veterinarian, and as it's a specialized bird hospital, the way she holds the birds is incomparably more stable than other places, which is a big plus.

Once, during a health checkup, my conure pecked at some droppings in the transport cage.
When I, the owner, said, "There's some droppings on his beak; it might get on your hand. I'm sorry," she calmly and gently moistened a cotton swab and quickly wiped it clean, as if it were nothing.

It was just a small incident, but as an owner, I wanted to wipe it off immediately, so I was very happy.

She doesn't overreact, but I think she's a trustworthy and caring veterinarian.

I know there are different ways of interpreting things, but I feel confident entrusting my conure to this veterinarian in the future.

I'm glad they're open on Sundays. My regular vet is closed on Sundays, so this was my first time here. The receptionist was very polite and even came out to the waiting room to check on me. I was curious about this female doctor based on online reviews, but her tone is rather detached, so I think some people might find her cold. However, she explained everything carefully during the examination, and she even washed the blood-stained perch for me. She was very attentive and I felt she was a very trustworthy doctor.

I will never take my pet birds there again. They're always making excuses. I didn't get to see the inspection, so I don't know the truth. I was such a fool to take them to a place like this. I can't stop regretting it.

The vet is very kind and caring towards birds. You can feel his love for birds even in the examination room, and I feel completely at ease entrusting my bird to him. I will continue to bring my bird in for regular checkups.

I received a second opinion from this clinic.

My bird fell ill, and I immediately took it to the hospital, but it hadn't improved the next day. I called to request a second opinion, and they were able to see my bird urgently.

I've been to four different avian veterinary hospitals before, but the examination, treatment, and diagnosis were all very quick, and I thought it was better for a sick bird to have the examination over quickly.

On the way home, my bird showed signs of improvement, so I'm glad I took it for a second opinion.

The cost of the examination, tests, and medication seemed reasonable, or perhaps even a little on the cheap.

Even during consultation hours, if the appointments are fully booked, even emergency cases cannot be seen.

It doesn't seem like I can make this my regular vet.

Although he is the head veterinarian and I can see he is used to birds, I felt he handled them roughly.

Other veterinarians at bird hospitals handle them very carefully...

His tone is very direct, which comes across as harsh.

I think he has a lot of knowledge about birds.

The doctor is still young, so I think he has a lot of potential. If he were more mindful of that, I think it would become an even better hospital.

The diagnosis was thorough, but even though I was so worried about my sick child that I desperately took him to the doctor, they said why they didn't notice sooner and that they didn't know how long he would last.
Of course, I loved him very much and played with him every day. I thought something was wrong and took him to the doctor right away.
Of course, a doctor might have noticed sooner.
When your child is sick is the most difficult thing. To be blamed in that way at such a time doesn't seem like I'll ever recover.

Recently, my parakeet accidentally swallowed some metal and suddenly started vomiting and couldn't eat.

After that, I took him to this hospital, and after a week of hospitalization, he's now recovered and is slowly getting better. He still needs medication every day, but I truly owe his recovery to the doctors.

I can't thank them enough. If I hadn't taken him to this hospital at that time, I don't think we'd be able to be together now.

This is a wonderful hospital that treats birds as cherished family members. Thank you so much.

When I took my Bunta to the vet, he gave me a thorough explanation of the treatment plan and other details, and I could tell that he really loves birds. He's a trustworthy doctor. Bunta has crossed the rainbow bridge, but I would like to take my birds there again if they are unwell in the future.

A new veterinary clinic specializing in birds opened, and I took my birds there a few times. The person who answered the phone was kind and helpful.

However, I felt like I was being scolded by the head veterinarian and his wife, who I believe were his wife. It was really scary.

I was considering making them my regular vet, and when I went to ask about breeding, I was asked in a condescending tone, "Are you confident you can properly feed your chicks even in the middle of the night?" I was quite shocked.

They were all smiles to regulars, but it felt like they were telling new patients never to come back.

I've decided I won't be going back there.

I took my Java sparrow to the vet.

I received a packet of medication costing 250 yen on my first visit.

I was told that the medication wasn't suitable and that I should switch to another one, so the original medication was discarded.

I was told the same thing on my next visit.

I stopped going after the fifth visit. Changing the medication didn't make it any better. Each visit cost about 10,000 yen.

But it didn't get any better.

They diagnose quickly, but they keep changing the medication, hoping it will work. It's like they're experimenting on the bird rather than selecting and prescribing an effective medication.

I'd gladly spend the money if it made things better, but it just cost money and stressed the bird.

I thought it was convenient because it was close, but I won't be going back.

I noticed a bulge under my bird's right leg and wondered what it was. I consulted online (justanswer) and was diagnosed with an abdominal wall hernia. I was stunned, but I decided to see Dr. Takagi at Osaka Bird Hospital. An X-ray revealed that it wasn't an abdominal wall hernia, but simply air buildup. I was relieved. He said he'd remove the air and treat it, and the bird's stomach collapsed and returned to normal. That was a huge relief.

I learned that Dr. Takagi is an honest person who only treats what needs to be done, and is far from being a money-making doctor, as some other reviews have suggested. He was thorough in his explanations and took great care with my bird. He treated my bird with the same dedication and compassion as if it were his own. His kind and thorough examinations are worthy of trust. I'll continue to send him to his clinic, and I'm convinced I can trust him as my regular doctor. He also helped me with the cost of my bird's treatment. I'm so grateful. The last photo was taken 40 days later.
I'm completely devastated.
Thank you so much.
They will carefully examine the bird's condition and provide treatment accordingly.
Thanks to this product, the old bird that could only move with its beak on the ground has turned negative and recovered. It's now very energetic and can fly again.

[Update added at the bottom, March 2025]

I already have a long-standing family veterinarian, but they have days off, of course.

I wanted to visit this clinic as well, since I knew I could get checked anytime.

I was thinking of taking my bird for a health check-up once things had settled down after the clinic opened, when, unexpectedly, my bird chewed on a cord, so I called immediately. They accepted me as an emergency patient. Thank you so much. I had learned from books that metal poisoning is dangerous, and I've been careful for over 20 years of keeping birds, so it had never happened before. However, my parakeet, whose lower body had become paralyzed, could only brace itself, but somehow it had managed to stretch to reach a cord that was in a position where it couldn't reach without stretching (perhaps it found it thrilling? Or fun?), and it had chewed on it while I was away at work.

This was the first time something like this had happened, and I was panicking on the phone, but the receptionist handled it calmly. Thank you so much.

The doctor who examined my bird was a man (the head veterinarian?).

I also attended the open house, and at that time I got the impression that the doctor was a serious and dedicated person, and that impression remained the same during the examination.

Perhaps for people who keep birds with a more relaxed attitude, his seriousness might seem a little intimidating.

The examination was smooth, and the bird seemed more comfortable than at its regular vet.

The result was that the bird had swallowed metal, so medication was prescribed, and a follow-up examination was scheduled once the medication ran out.

After prefacing with "This isn't an immediate issue," the doctor said, "This bird's bone structure puts a lot of strain on its organs, so it will likely need heart medication and other things in the future."

I was surprised that he could tell all that just from the X-ray!

For those planning to visit for the first time, I recommend going with the understanding that the doctor has a cool demeanor. He is passionate about birds, though.

[Additional Information Below]
I took my cockatiel in as an emergency case after it suffered two open fractures of its wing bones due to panic.

The doctor let out a deep sigh and said, "A normal bird can do this, but this one can't. There's nothing we can do." He said it would only last two or three days. I understood the explanation, and honestly, I was prepared for the worst since she'd come close to death so many times. They prescribed some treatment and medication, hoping for a slim chance of survival. They scheduled an appointment for a week later, saying a check-up would be necessary if she survived.

I asked if I should cancel the appointment if she passed away, and they said, "If it's too painful for you, you don't have to."

I thought to myself, "There's nothing more we can do," and realized that the doctor, who became a physician to save lives, must feel even more helpless than I do as the owner... so I thanked them and left.

Miraculously, she's still alive! While her condition is still critical, when I went for the check-up, the receptionist looked surprised, and the doctor smiled slightly, saying she'd done well, which relieved me too.

We also confirmed the future treatment plan.

If she's still alive, I think we'll need to continue taking her to the vet for a while.

She's had two pelvic fractures from paper bone, followed by paralysis of her lower body, pancreatitis, and now an open fracture.

Perhaps because her legs don't move, she can't fly, meaning the pain from her wing injuries was less severe, but the shock wasn't as great. I'll be relying on your services frequently for a while longer. Thank you in advance.

I am incredibly grateful to Dr. Takagi for taking care of my Java sparrow and budgie.

I initially came to him for a second opinion on my Java sparrow, but he instantly identified a disease that other hospitals couldn't find, and now my bird is so energetic it's almost a handful!

My budgie had developed PBFD, and I was filled with anxiety because the internet was full of negative information, such as how difficult the treatment was and that my bird might not live to its full lifespan. However, Dr. Takagi examined my bird carefully every week, constantly giving me positive remarks about how healthy it seemed and how its weight was good.

Thanks to Dr. Takagi, the symptoms have now cleared up, and my bird is so energetic that it's almost a handful for me to handle!

I am truly grateful for his sincere and dedicated care throughout the process, especially considering the high risk to the hospital due to the highly contagious nature of the disease.

Also, because my bird's symptoms could potentially spread to other birds, I scheduled its appointment for the very last slot, and the thorough disinfection of the examination room after each visit gave me great peace of mind.

Thank you so much, Dr. Takagi.

I can now confidently continue my long life with my birds.

For some reason, the leg band on my white-bellied parakeet had tightened, and he saved the leg just before it was on the verge of necrosis. The leg was so swollen that there was no space left for the band, but he patiently cut the band little by little without anesthesia and successfully removed it. You can feel his love in everything, from the way he treats the bird to the way he talks to the bird and the words he uses to address its owner. He is a wonderful director.

What's been bothering me is that the doctor never seems to remember the details of the previous examination.

Also, I feel uneasy because what he's saying now is different from what he said before.

With these various uneasy feelings, the next appointment arrived.

Ah, it's different from last time again...

He said he would do a detailed examination, but this time it was just a physical examination with no proper explanation of the bird's current condition.

And he prescribed a long-term supply of antibiotics.

All he said was, "Please continue the medication."

The explanation of the examination is truly insufficient.

...Ah, I feel uneasy again.

As a pet owner, all I want is to protect this little life I love.

I've been going to this hospital because there aren't many specialized bird hospitals, but I've recently been thinking about switching hospitals.

It's a small thing, but this doctor doesn't get involved at all when I put the bird's carrier back into the bag after the examination, haha.
I've been to three different animal hospitals in the past, and all the doctors there would have a little conversation with the owner, talk to the animal, and help out.

While it was time to put the items back in the bag, I remained silent and quietly typed away on my keyboard.

What I'm trying to say isn't that I need help, but rather that I wish there was a little more communication...
That time...it felt kind of strange, haha.

However, I appreciate that this hospital properly accepts emergency patients.

The reception staff's service was also excellent.
I'm so grateful that a bird-specializing hospital has opened nearby. The doctors and receptionists are very kind.

I'm always indebted to Dr. Marina for her help with health checkups and other matters.

She's been very supportive with the dietary restrictions to suppress my Java sparrow's estrus cycle, and it looks like it's going to work! I'm truly grateful.

This is a very trustworthy hospital for my birds and me!!
